How do you get a root shell via UART on an embedded device?

UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter) is a serial communication interface that often exposes a root shell or bootloader on embedded devices. Process: 1) Identify UART pads on PCB — typically 4 pins labeled TX, RX, GND, VCC or near a row of test pads. Use multimeter continuity mode to find GND. Use oscilloscope or multimeter in DC mode to find TX (signal fluctuates at boot). 2) Determine baud rate: logic analyzer with Sigrok/PulseView or use minicom auto-baud detection. Common rates: 115200, 57600, 38400, 9600. 3) Connect: USB-UART adapter (CP2102, CH340, FTDI) — TX→RX, RX→TX, GND→GND, do NOT connect VCC unless device is bus-powered. 4) Open terminal: picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyUSB0. 5) Interrupt boot (U-Boot): press any key during countdown to drop into bootloader. From bootloader: setenv bootargs 'console=ttyS0,115200 root=/dev/mtdblock2 init=/bin/sh'. bootm to boot into single-user mode.

Explain how to dump SPI flash memory from an embedded device.

SPI flash contains firmware — extracting it enables offline analysis, reverse engineering, and modification. Method 1 (in-circuit): 1) Identify SPI flash chip on PCB (common: Winbond W25Q series, Macronix MX25L series). Read chip markings. 2) Attach SOIC8 clip to chip or use fine-pitch probes on pins. 3) Connect to CH341A programmer (most common, ~$5) or Bus Pirate. 4) flashrom -p ch341a_spi -r firmware.bin to dump. Method 2 (desolder): hot air gun to remove chip → TL866II programmer with correct adapter socket → flashrom or minipro -p CHIP_NAME -r firmware.bin. Post-extraction: binwalk -e firmware.bin to extract filesystems. strings firmware.bin | grep -i password for credentials. Ghidra or IDA Pro for firmware reverse engineering. firmwalker for automated credential/config extraction. If encrypted: extract keys from bootloader or RAM dump.

How do you identify and exploit JTAG on an embedded device?

JTAG (Joint Test Action Group) provides low-level hardware debugging access — essentially GDB at the silicon level. Step 1 — Find JTAG pins: Look for unpopulated headers, test pads in rows. Use JTAGulator (automated) or JTAGenum (Arduino sketch) to identify pinout from suspected pads. JTAGulator connects to all candidate pins and scans for JTAG signals. Step 2 — Connect: Use OpenOCD with your interface (Tigard, J-Link, Black Magic Probe). Config file for target CPU: openocd -f interface/jlink.cfg -f target/at91sam9.cfg. Step 3 — Debug: OpenOCD exposes GDB server on port 3333. Connect: arm-none-eabi-gdb, target remote :3333. Now you have full debug access — read RAM, set breakpoints, dump memory regions, modify registers. Step 4 — Extract secrets: dump_image ram.bin 0x00000000 0x08000000 in OpenOCD telnet session. Analyze with Ghidra/Binwalk.

What is fault injection / voltage glitching and how does it bypass security?

Fault injection induces hardware errors to bypass security checks (secure boot, PIN verification, encryption). Voltage glitching: briefly drop VCC to create a processor glitch at a precise moment — causing it to skip an instruction or return wrong value from a comparison. Target scenario: MCU checks PIN code and branches based on result. A glitch at the comparison instruction causes it to always take the 'correct' branch. Tools: ChipWhisperer (professional, Python API), DIY: TS100 iron tip connected to GPIO for EMFI (electromagnetic fault injection). Process: 1) Identify target instruction via JTAG/debug or power trace analysis. 2) Set up trigger — target device signals start of sensitive operation via GPIO or power consumption spike. 3) Inject glitch at precise offset from trigger. 4) Automate: ChipWhisperer scripting tries thousands of glitch parameters (width, offset, voltage). Applications: extract encrypted firmware, bypass secure boot, extract HSM keys, bypass smartcard PIN verification.

Explain side-channel attacks and differential power analysis (DPA).

Side-channel attacks extract cryptographic keys by measuring physical emissions (power consumption, electromagnetic radiation, timing) during cryptographic operations. DPA specifically analyzes power traces during cryptographic computation. Process: 1) Collect power traces: ChipWhisperer with SAKURA or target board — capture N traces (typically 1000-10000) during AES encryption with known plaintexts. 2) Hypothesis: for each possible key byte value (0-255), predict intermediate value (e.g., SubBytes output). 3) Correlation: compute Pearson correlation between predicted power model and actual traces. Correct key byte produces highest correlation at the correct clock cycle. 4) Repeat for all 16 AES-128 key bytes independently — recover full 128-bit key. ChipWhisperer Jupyter notebooks provide ready-to-run DPA attacks. Counter-measures: masking schemes, random delays, hardware AES accelerators with built-in DPA resistance. EMFI (Electromagnetic) variant uses near-field H-field probe placed directly on IC.

How do you hack automotive CAN bus systems?

CAN bus is the communication backbone connecting all ECUs (Engine Control Unit, ABS, airbags, infotainment) in modern vehicles. Physical access: OBD-II port (under dash) or direct access to CAN wires. Tools: USB2CAN adapter with SocketCAN (Linux), Wireshark with socketcan plugin, python-can library. Recon: cansniffer -c can0 to monitor live traffic, log a drive and analyze patterns. canreplay can0 -f logfile to replay captured traffic. Fuzzing: cangen can0 -I 7DF -L 8 -D r to send random diagnostic frames on OBD-II broadcast ID. Target scenario: keyless entry — capture and replay rolling codes (requires sub-GHz radio for RF attacks). Remote attack vector: infotainment unit (often has WiFi/Bluetooth and is connected to CAN bus). Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek's Jeep Cherokee remote exploit path: cellular → infotainment → CAN bus → steering/brakes. Tools: CANBUS Triple, CANalyzer (professional), ICSim for safe practice.

What is the Bus Pirate and how do you use it for hardware hacking?

Bus Pirate is a universal serial protocol interface for UART, SPI, I2C, 1-Wire, JTAG. Though outdated (superseded by Tigard/HydraBus), still widely available. Connect via USB → /dev/ttyUSB0 at 115200 8N1. Interface menu: HiZ, 1-WIRE, UART, I2C, SPI, 2WIRE, 3WIRE, KEYB, LCD, PIC. SPI mode example: m 5 (SPI), set speed 1MHz, select output type 3.3V. Commands: [0x9F] reads flash JEDEC ID. For SPI flash dump: [0x03 0x00 0x00 0x00 r:1000] reads 1000 bytes from address 0. UART pass-through: transparent UART bridge mode for sniffing/injecting. I2C enumeration: (1) 0xA0 sends address 0x50 (EEPROM range scan). Practical use: dump EEPROM from devices with chip in-circuit, sniff I2C communication between MCU and sensors, inject UART commands into embedded Linux console.

How do you perform firmware extraction from a router or IoT device?

Multi-method approach — try easiest first: Method 1 (web interface): Check if admin console has firmware download option. Also check upgrade function — intercept with Burp Suite and redirect to /dev/null to trigger firmware exposure. Method 2 (UART): Boot device with serial console attached, get root shell, dd if=/dev/mtdblock0 of=/tmp/fw.bin, then tftp/netcat to exfiltrate. Method 3 (SPI/NAND flash): identify flash chip, use flashrom or CH341A to dump. Method 4 (TFTP/update server): intercept OTA update process — firmware often downloads via HTTP with no integrity verification. Method 5 (binwalk from vendor): manufacturers often post firmware downloads on support pages. Post-extraction: binwalk -Mre firmware.bin (recursive extraction of all nested archives), firmwalker.sh for automated vulnerability hunting, Firmadyne for full QEMU emulation, FAT (Firmware Analysis Toolkit) for automated CVE scanning.

Explain how to use HackRF for RF OSINT and signal analysis.

HackRF One is a software-defined radio (SDR) that covers 1MHz-6GHz, capable of both receive and transmit. Setup: install GNU Radio, GnuRadio Companion, SDR++ or GQRX for visual spectrum analysis. Initial recon: open GQRX, scan spectrum around target frequency (e.g., 433MHz for ISM band devices, 315MHz for older US key fobs, 868MHz for European IoT, 2.4GHz for WiFi/Bluetooth/Zigbee). Capture and analyze: hackrf_transfer -r capture.cs8 -f 433920000 -s 2000000 to capture IQ data. Import into URH (Universal Radio Hacker) for demodulation and protocol analysis. Replay attacks: hackrf_transfer -t capture.cs8 -f 433920000 -s 2000000 -x 40 to transmit. Key targets: garage door openers (fixed-code exploitable, rolling-code requires TPMS/RollJam), wireless alarm sensors, smart meters (AMR protocol), tire pressure sensors (TPMS broadcasts vehicle ID + tire pressure — passive vehicle tracking).

What is QEMU and how do you use it to emulate IoT firmware?

QEMU emulates CPU architectures (ARM, MIPS, PowerPC) used in IoT devices, enabling dynamic analysis without physical hardware. Approach: 1) Extract firmware (binwalk -e firmware.bin), identify root filesystem. 2) Determine architecture: file ./squashfs-root/bin/busybox or readelf -h binary. 3) Install qemu-user-static for user-mode or full system emulation. User-mode (fast): copy qemu-arm-static to extracted root, chroot and run binaries. sudo chroot squashfs-root/ /usr/bin/qemu-arm-static /bin/sh. 4) Full system: use Firmadyne or FAT — automated setup with network support for testing web interfaces. 5) Once running: access web interface on emulated network, run dynamic analysis tools (strace, ltrace, gdb), test for vulnerabilities. Tools: Firmadyne, FirmAE (improved), QEMU + Buildroot for custom kernel environments, unicorn engine for selective code emulation without full OS.

How do you use OpenOCD for JTAG debugging and memory extraction?

OpenOCD (Open On-Chip Debugger) is the standard open-source JTAG/SWD debugging tool. Install: sudo apt install openocd. Configuration: requires two cfg files — interface (your debugger hardware) and target (the chip). openocd -f interface/tigard.cfg -f target/stm32f1x.cfg. Connect via telnet (port 4444) or GDB (port 3333). Key telnet commands: halt — stop CPU execution, resume — continue execution, reset halt — reset and stop at first instruction, dump_image output.bin 0x08000000 0x00020000 — dump Flash memory to file, mdw 0x20000000 — read word from RAM address, mww 0x20000000 0xDEADBEEF — write to memory. For ARM Cortex-M: targets often have IDCODE readable without halt. Flash extraction: stm32f1x unlock 0 to disable readout protection (on some chips this erases), then dump_image. GDB: arm-none-eabi-gdb then target remote :3333 for full symbolic debugging if firmware has debug symbols.

Explain ChipWhisperer and its use in hardware security research.

ChipWhisperer is the industry-standard platform for side-channel analysis (SCA) and fault injection research. Hardware components: CW-Lite (entry level), CW-Pro, NANO (ultra cheap). Target boards: UFO target (generic), dedicated SAM4S, STM32 targets. Software: Python-based Jupyter notebooks. SCA workflow: 1) Connect ChipWhisperer to target, connect trigger GPIO. 2) scope = cw.scope(); target = cw.target(scope). 3) Capture N power traces during AES: trace = scope.get_last_trace(). 4) Load into SPA (Simple Power Analysis) or run CPA (Correlation Power Analysis) automatically via ChipWhisperer analyzer. Pre-built attacks: AES SCA, RSA SCA, password bypass via timing. Fault injection: scope.glitch.clk_src, offset, width, repeat control glitch parameters. Automated campaigns: scripts iterate glitch parameters until target breaks out of secure boot or returns incorrect comparison result. Resources: chipwhisperer.io tutorials, cw hardware wiki.

How do you identify and attack I2C devices on embedded hardware?

I2C is a two-wire serial protocol (SDA + SCL) commonly used for EEPROMs, sensors, and displays. Identification: use oscilloscope or logic analyzer to observe 7-bit address transactions at start of communication. Common I2C devices: 24CXX EEPROMs (0x50-0x57), RTC modules (0x68/0x6F), temperature sensors (0x48-0x4F), port expanders (0x20-0x27). Attack tools: Bus Pirate in I2C mode, Tigard, or i2cdetect tool in Linux. i2cdetect -y 1 scans all 127 addresses. i2cdump -y 1 0x50 dumps EEPROM at address 0x50 in hex. i2cset -y 1 0x50 0x00 0xFF writes 0xFF to byte 0 of EEPROM. Attack scenarios: 1) EEPROM stores product serial/license key — read and clone. 2) EEPROM stores configuration including WiFi passwords in plaintext. 3) TPM-like security chips on I2C can sometimes be attacked with glitching at the I2C transaction level. 4) Bitbang I2C from microcontroller to bypass clock stretching protection.

What are the best logic analyzers for hardware hacking and how do you use them?

Recommended hardware: DSLogic Plus (16ch, up to 400MHz, best value at ~$150), Saleae Logic 8/16 (professional, $500-1500), Generic 8ch Saleae clone from AliExpress ($10, limited to 24MHz). Software: Sigrok/PulseView (free, supports all hardware via libsigrok), Saleae Logic 2 (best UX, proprietary), DSView for DSLogic. Usage: 1) Connect probes to target signal lines (SDA/SCL for I2C, MOSI/MISO/CLK/CS for SPI, TX/RX for UART). 2) Set sample rate to 4-10x higher than the communication frequency. 3) Capture traffic during target operation. 4) In PulseView: Add Protocol Decoder (I2C/SPI/UART/1-Wire/CAN). 5) Decoder automatically parses protocol and shows human-readable data. Use case: captured I2C transaction shows EEPROM write of 'password123'. SPI decoder shows flash read of encryption key. UART decoder reveals boot log with filesystem layout.

How do you perform electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI)?

EMFI uses a tightly focused electromagnetic pulse to flip bits or disrupt CPU execution at a precise location. Unlike voltage glitching, EMFI can target specific silicon regions without circuit modification. DIY setup: 1) Build EM probe: coil of magnet wire (5-10 turns, ~5mm diameter) on ferrite core. 2) Drive coil with high-voltage pulse: MOSFET switch + 100V-400V capacitor bank triggered by microcontroller. 3) Connect trigger from target (GPIO or power trigger). 4) Mount probe on XY stage for precise positioning over IC. 5) Automate with ChipWhisperer EMFI module or custom Arduino controller. Professional tools: Langer EMV-Technik probes, Riscure VC Glitcher. Targeting: scan target IC surface systematically while glitching — monitor for faults in output (wrong calculation result, skipped instruction, premature return from security check). Best targets: boot ROM security checks, cryptographic function outputs, PIN comparison routines. Key paper: 'Fault Attacks on Secure Chips: From Theory to Practice' (CHES proceedings).

How do you reverse engineer unknown serial protocols on hardware?

Systematic protocol RE workflow: 1) Capture raw data: logic analyzer on all data lines, capture during known operations (power on, button press, data transfer). 2) Visual analysis: look for patterns in PulseView — repeated bytes (sync/magic numbers), framing (start/stop bytes), periodic structure. 3) Frequency analysis: count byte values — 0x00 and 0xFF are common padding, frequently repeated bytes may be commands. 4) Correlation: press a button, observe what changes in the capture. Repeat for all buttons/functions. 5) Use URH (Universal Radio Hacker) for RF protocols or Scapy for network-like protocols. 6) Statistical analysis: measure packet length distribution, inter-packet timing. 7) Known protocol identification: use Sigrok protocol decoders, check against known industrial protocols (Modbus, DMX512, SMBus). 8) Differential analysis: compare captures for similar operations — what changes? Command byte shifts? Checksum updates? 9) Write custom protocol decoder in Sigrok Python.
